scale.summary: Label scale, 25-minute budget, everything under /tmp/store-layout/scale/ (harness/main.go, harness/trie/main.go, harness/occupancy.py + trie_model.py, results-50k.tsv, results-trie-stats.txt, results-occupancy.txt; six 50k-object stores A-trie-d2, B-p4, C-p5, D-p6, E-p4-p6, F-flat; trie/d1, d2, d3). ID generator verified byte-for-byte against c4 1.0.18 on 4 inputs. Measured at 50k objects on warm APFS: all six layouts look alike for lookups (2.8-4.0 us hit); the differences are directory count and enumeration (A/B 182 dirs, 0.05 s walk; D/E about 43.7k dirs, 1.3 s walk, 25x; 1.7x slower to create). du -sk is 0 for every layout (APFS keeps empty files and directories in the metadata B-tree), so the directory cost shows only as summed directory st_size: 1.6 MiB for A/B/F, 2.2 MiB for C, 5.7 MiB for D/E. Stat counts: the 1.0.18 reader costs depth+2 stats on a hit (3/4/5 at depth 1/2/3); the any-depth reader done deepest-first costs the same on a hit and about 2 extra stats on a miss (4/6/6.2); done top-down it costs 2 extra on every hit. Occupancy math (exact prefix probabilities, Poisson bins; P(id[2]='6') = 2.3%, 182/6,370/222,950 reachable folded bins at 2/3/4 chars) says no fixed-prefix layout stays in the 100-50,000 band across 10^3-10^15, and that the adaptive trie's real problem is not the ceiling but its split shape: a 4,096 threshold with a 1,225-way lowercased fan-out drops a leaf to about 3 objects per directory the moment it splits, so at 10^6 objects the trie is 141k directories averaging 7 objects, and at 10^9 it is 75M directories averaging 14. Threshold 65,536 keeps every size from 10^6 up at 448-6,900 mean (dipping to 71 at 10^7) but breaks FAT32. Ceilings (cited): ext4 and NTFS cap at about 4.29 billion files per filesystem, ext4 per directory about 10-12M entries (6 billion with large_dir); XFS 2^64 files; ZFS 2^48 entries per directory, files unlimited; APFS 2^63 files per volume. The single-filesystem store stops being sensible around 10^8-10^9 objects (ext4/NTFS cap, inode budget, and tens of millions of directories to walk), and the same lowercased prefix rule partitions cleanly: a table from level-1 (182) or level-2 (222,950) prefixes to volumes/buckets, routed from the ID alone, which is new code in MultiStore.

findings.fact: The harness encoder ("c4" + base58 of SHA-512, left-padded with '1' to 88 chars, via math/big) produced byte-identical IDs to `c4 id` for the empty input, "hello", "The quick brown fox" and 8 zero bytes, with C4_STORE=/tmp/store-layout/scale/verify-store.
findings.evidence: /tmp/store-layout/scale/harness/main.go (`./harness id < file`); e.g. empty input -> c459dsjfscH38cYeXXYogktxf4Cd9ibshE3BHUo6a58hBXmRQdZrAkZzsWcbWtDg5oQstpDuni4Hirj75GEmTc1sFT from both.
findings.consequence_for_rule: Synthetic IDs used below have the real distribution (including the skewed third character), so the occupancy math is about real c4 IDs, not uniform strings.

findings.topic: 50,000 empty objects, six layouts, warm APFS (measured)
findings.fact: create_s / dirs / hit-lookup us / miss-lookup us / enumerate_s: A trie c4/xx: 2.88 / 184 / 2.78 / 8.74 / 0.054. B id[0:4]: 2.79 / 183 / 3.19 / 8.59 / 0.052. C id[0:5]: 3.14 / 6,316 / 3.40 / 8.45 / 0.228. D id[0:6]: 4.76 / 43,695 / 3.29 / 7.82 / 1.276. E id[0:4]/id[4:6]: 4.89 / 43,877 / 3.50 / 7.84 / 1.367. F flat: 2.66 / 1 / 3.95 / 16.55 / 0.075. 10,000 hits found 10,000/10,000 in every layout. du -sk reported 0k for all six trees; summed directory st_size (APFS reports 32 bytes per entry) was 1,580 KiB for A and B, 1,563 KiB for F, 2,155 KiB for C, 5,659 KiB for D and 5,676 KiB for E.
findings.evidence: /tmp/store-layout/scale/results-50k.tsv; stores under /tmp/store-layout/scale/{A-trie-d2,B-p4,C-p5,D-p6,E-p4-p6,F-flat}/; df shows /tmp on APFS (/dev/disk3s5).
findings.consequence_for_rule: At 50k objects lookups by computed path are indistinguishable across layouts (all 3-4 us hit, 8 us miss; flat miss 16.5 us is the only outlier). The layouts differ in what a full walk costs: D and E are 25x slower to enumerate and 1.7x slower to create because of 44k mostly-single-object directories. A and B are equivalent at this size; A is B with a c4/ level inserted.

findings.topic: Stat calls per lookup: 1.0.18 reader vs any-depth reader (measured, 20,000-object tries at depth 1, 2, 3)
findings.fact: reader1018 (descend while 2-char dir exists, then stat file): hit 3.00 / 4.00 / 5.00 stats at depth 1/2/3 (= depth+2); miss 3.00 / 4.00 / 4.11. anyDepthDeepestFirst (same descent, then check each level upward on a miss): hit 3.00 / 4.00 / 5.00 (identical to 1.0.18); miss 4.00 / 6.00 / 6.22. anyDepthTopDown (stat file then dir at each level from the root): hit 3.00 / 5.00 / 7.00; miss 4.00 / 6.00 / 6.22. Microseconds per lookup (warm, noisy +-30%, 5,000 lookups each): 1.0.18 hit 5.8 / 11.0 / 22.3, miss 13.1 / 17.8 / 17.2; deepest-first hit 9.2 / 8.2 / 14.7, miss 10.4 / 16.1 / 16.8; top-down hit 8.3 / 14.1 / 28.8, miss 18.1 / 24.7 / 24.4.
findings.consequence_for_rule: The any-depth invariant is free on a hit if implemented deepest-first (check the deepest existing directory first, as 1.0.18 does, then climb). It costs exactly one extra stat per level only on a miss (about +2 at depth 2). The top-down order the draft describes (root first) adds 2 stats to every hit at depth 2 and should not be the reference implementation. Both any-depth misses are still far cheaper than the 1.0.18 fold fallback (11-13 stats per the compat ground result).

findings.topic: Reachable folded prefixes and the third-character skew (exact)
findings.fact: 58^88 exceeds 2^512, so the third ID character is '1'-'5' with probability 0.1954 each and '6' with 0.0231; under '6' only a tail of later characters exists. Exact folded bin counts: id[2:4] 182 (not 210), id[2:5] 6,370, id[2:6] 222,950. Bin probabilities are uneven by up to 2.3x at every level because a lowercased letter present in both cases carries 2/58 and a digit or i/l/o carries 1/58: id[2:4] bins range 2.89e-3 to 6.74e-3; id[2:6] bins 1.00e-6 to 8.01e-6. Deeper 2-char levels split 1,225 ways with three weights (1, 2 and 4 /3364: 144, 552, 529 bins).
findings.evidence: /tmp/store-layout/scale/harness/occupancy.py folded_bins(); printed `sum=1.000000` for n=2,3,4; matches the 182 directories observed in both real stores (compat ground result) and in store A.
findings.consequence_for_rule: The expected maximum directory is about 1.23x the mean at level 1 and up to 4x the smallest sibling at deeper levels, so any threshold or ceiling must be checked against the heaviest bin (6.74e-3 of all objects at level 1), not the mean.

findings.topic: Occupancy of the fixed one-level layouts (model, Poisson bins)
findings.consequence_for_rule: No fixed-prefix layout covers the range. Each is unruly at the low end: C puts a 1,000-object store in 914 directories; D/E put a 10,000-object store in 9,721 directories and a 200,000-object store in about 130,000 (matches the 120k measured in the compat result). B is the only fixed layout tidy at the low end and it tops out near 10^7. Only an adaptive layout can satisfy both ends, which the draft already concluded; the numbers above are the quantified reason.

findings.topic: Adaptive trie at threshold 4,096: depth, directories, lookup cost (model)
findings.evidence: /tmp/store-layout/scale/results-occupancy.txt section 'A adaptive trie, threshold 4096'; model in /tmp/store-layout/scale/harness/trie_model.py (splits on expected count, so '1-2' means bins straddle the threshold).
findings.consequence_for_rule: The trie has no ceiling and reaches only depth 4-5 at 10^15 (6.5 stats per hit), confirming the draft on the high end. But it is NOT inside the sane band: a 4,096 threshold with a 1,225-way lowercased fan-out means a leaf drops to about 3.3 objects per directory the moment it splits. The store is tidy up to about 600k objects, then between 1M and 10M it is 141k-223k directories averaging 7-45 objects, and the same collapse recurs at every later split (10^9: 75M dirs of 14; 10^12: 1.45e11 dirs of 7). The threshold is 3x smaller than the fan-out; a sane split needs threshold about 100x fan-out, or a smaller fan-out.

findings.topic: Adaptive trie at threshold 65,536 (the comparison threshold)
findings.fact: 10^3 and 10^4: flat. 10^6: depth 1, 183 dirs, 5,495 mean, max 6,943. 10^7: 1-2, 141k dirs, mean 71, max 34,110. 10^8: depth 2, 223k dirs, mean 449, max 921. 10^9: depth 2, 4,485 mean, max 8,390. 10^12: depth 3, 273M dirs, mean 3,662, max 10,060. 10^15: depth 4, 3.3e11 dirs, mean 2,989, max 12,018, 7 singletons. Hit stats 2 / 2 / 3 / 3.77 / 4 / 4 / 5 / 6.
findings.consequence_for_rule: Threshold 65,536 keeps the whole range from 10^6 up inside or near the 100-50,000 band (one dip to a mean of 71 right after the first split at 10^7), with 10-100x fewer directories than 4,096 at every size above 10^6 and one fewer level at 10^12-10^15. The cost: it exceeds FAT32's 7,800-entry cap (portability result) and a 65k-entry flat root before the first split; the measured 50k flat directory was fine on APFS (3.95 us hit). If FAT32 is a target the alternative that fixes the shape without raising the threshold is a smaller fan-out per level (a 1-character step is 35-way; 4,096/35 = 117 per child after a split), which is a format change and was not measured.

findings.fact: ext4: about 4 billion files per filesystem, fixed at creation (inode count); 10-12 million entries per directory with the default 2-level HTree (2 GB directory at 4 KiB blocks), about 6 billion per directory with large_dir (Linux 4.12+); no subdirectory limit beyond directory size. XFS: 2^64 files per filesystem (infobox, flagged citation-needed); no stated per-directory entry cap, directories are B+ trees. ZFS: 2^48 entries per directory, files per dataset unlimited. APFS: 2^63 (9,223,372,036,854,775,808) files per volume, no stated per-directory limit. NTFS: 4,294,967,295 (2^32 - 1) files per volume. From the portability result: FAT32 8,191 objects per directory at 90-character names; exFAT 1,048,576 per directory with linear scans.
findings.evidence: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ext4 (Limits infobox; Features, 'Unlimited number of subdirectories'); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/XFS (infobox); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ZFS (capacity limits); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_File_System; https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NTFS (infobox); https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/storage/file-server/ntfs-overview gives volume size only (8 PB max, 2^32-1 clusters).
findings.consequence_for_rule: No layout on one ext4 or NTFS volume can exceed about 4.29x10^9 objects, and an ext4 volume formatted with the default inode ratio holds far fewer (one inode per 16 KiB of volume). Per-directory limits never bind the lowercased trie (max 6,943 per leaf at threshold 4,096 even at 10^15); they bind the fixed layouts B at about 10^9 (ext4 htree) and C at about 10^10.

findings.topic: Where a single-filesystem directory store stops being sensible, and partitioning by the same rule
findings.fact: Measured: enumerating 43.7k directories cost 1.3 s warm; the model puts the 4,096-threshold trie at 75M directories at 10^9 objects (about 40 minutes of warm directory reads at the measured rate, far more cold) and 223k directories from 10^7 to 10^8. ext4/NTFS hard cap at 4.29x10^9; APFS, XFS and ZFS do not cap. Directory metadata measured at 32 bytes per entry on APFS plus one inode per object (ext4 256 B each: 10^9 objects need 256 GB of inode table alone).
findings.evidence: results-50k.tsv enumerate column; results-occupancy.txt trie sections; ceilings above.
findings.consequence_for_rule: Somewhere between 10^8 and 10^9 objects a single-volume directory store is past the ext4/NTFS cap, past any reasonable full walk, and past the inode budget, regardless of layout. The lowercased-prefix rule partitions without a new concept: the prefix path is a pure function of the ID, so a routing table from level-1 names (182 bins of 0.29-0.67% each) or level-2 names (222,950 bins, about 4.5e-6 each) to volumes, buckets or stores is the same trie one level up, with each partition starting flat and deepening on its own. Routing is new code (MultiStore is ordered search today, per the compat result); on S3 no partitioning is needed since keys are flat and prefix throughput scales automatically (portability result).

findings.fact: All timings are warm-cache, empty files, APFS, 50k objects (the task cap) and single runs with roughly 30% noise visible between repeated conditions. The occupancy model splits on expected counts (deterministic), so a real store straddling a threshold has a mix of split and unsplit siblings; medians of the maximum use Poisson or normal approximations. The 2.3x level-1 and 4x deeper-level bin unevenness is exact. Directory metadata cost was taken from st_size because du reports 0 for empty files and directories on APFS. A first run of occupancy.py had a normalisation bug (bins summed to 0.04); it was fixed (`p = m * full`) and every table above is from the corrected run, whose bin sums print as 1.000000.
findings.consequence_for_rule: Treat the microsecond figures as order-of-magnitude and the stat counts, directory counts and occupancy means as exact. The decisive scale fact for the rule is the shape mismatch (threshold 4,096 vs fan-out 1,225), which does not depend on any timing.

draft.rule: From the store root, take the ID two characters at a time, ASCII-lowercased (c4, 4e, uw, ...), and step into that directory while it exists; the object is the file named by its full exact-case 90-character ID in the deepest directory reached, and is equally valid in any directory passed through on the way (a store with no directories is simply the flat case: <store>/<ID>). Formally: path_k(id) = <store>/lower(id[0:2])/lower(id[2:4])/.../lower(id[2k-2:2k])/<id> for k = 0..44; an object exists iff path_k(id) is a regular file for some k; the only directories that may exist are those on some ID's prefix path with exactly-2-character lowercase names. Nothing else is in the format: no marker file, no threshold, no fixed depth. On an object store (S3) the rule at k=0: key = <prefix><exact-case ID>.

parameters.name: Prefix width per level
parameters.choice: Exactly 2 characters at every level, including the first (which is therefore always the literal directory 'c4').
parameters.why: 2-character names can never be Windows reserved names (3- and 4-character ones can: con, com1); 2 is what every existing trie store and reader uses (1.0.18, master, c4py, imgbin, both real stores with 194,127 and 64,433 objects), so adoption is renames, not moves. The 1,225-way fan-out is coarse (scale: a leaf drops to ~3 objects/dir at split), but a 1-character level (35-way) is a clean break with every store and tool and was not measured; the coarse shape costs directory count, never correctness, and is bounded by the threshold choice below.

parameters.name: Fixed vs adaptive depth
parameters.choice: Adaptive: directories appear only where a writer chose to create them; readers derive nothing from the object count.
parameters.why: Scale occupancy math: no fixed prefix stays in the 100-50,000 objects/dir band across 10^3-10^15 (id[0:4] tops out ~10^7 on ext4 htree and 1.5M on FAT32; id[0:6] puts a 10k-object store in 9,721 directories). Adaptive has no ceiling (depth 4-5 at 10^15, 6.5 stats/hit) and a 1,000-object store has zero directories.

parameters.name: 'c4' in the directory name
parameters.choice: Yes, as the ordinary first 2-character level (every ID starts 'c4', so level 1 is always the directory c4/). Not a special case in code: it is lower(id[0:2]).
parameters.why: Both real stores are c4/XX/<ID>; dropping the level forces 194,127 object moves and breaks every reader. It costs 3 path characters and one directory, and it separates ID-named content from non-ID files at the root (journal, log.c4m, .ingest.*) once a store has split.

parameters.name: Case folding
parameters.choice: ASCII A-Z to a-z only, applied to directory names only; the object file name keeps exact case.
parameters.why: Base58 has no 'I' so lowercasing is locale-proof; uppercasing 'i' breaks under tr/az locales (portability). Lowercase is also what Samba recommends for large directories. Exact-case file names keep the ID recoverable from the path and keep S3 keys unchanged.

parameters.name: Split threshold
parameters.choice: NOT part of the format. It is a writer-local tuning parameter; the shared default is 4,096 files per directory (counting ID-named files only). A writer may also never split (imgbin, c4ts, c4d, Swift, C).
parameters.why: Under the any-depth invariant every reader reads a store produced at any threshold, so the number cannot create incompatibility and should not be frozen. 4,096 stays the default because it is FAT32-safe (8,191 entries at 90-char names; 2x margin) and is what all shipped writers do. The scale result shows 4,096 vs a 1,225-way fan-out gives an ugly middle (10^6-10^7 objects: 141k-223k directories averaging 7-45) and that 65,536 fixes the shape (448-6,900 mean from 10^6 up) but breaks FAT32/exFAT; a store on APFS/XFS/ZFS can be written at 65,536 today via SetSplitThreshold with no format change. What I gave up: tidy directory occupancy between the first split (~600k objects) and ~10^7, and at each later split boundary. Directory count there is 25x slower to enumerate (measured 1.3 s for 44k dirs) but lookups are unchanged (3-4 us at every layout).

parameters.name: Any-depth validity
parameters.choice: Adopted, with the reader order fixed as deepest-first (descend while the lowercase directory exists, stat the file there, then climb one level at a time).
parameters.why: Measured: deepest-first costs the same as 1.0.18 on a hit (depth+2 stats) and +1 stat per level only on a miss (4/6/6.2 at depth 1/2/3), far below the 1.0.18 fold fallback (11-13); top-down costs +2 on every hit at depth 2 and is rejected as the reference. Run tonight with 1.0.18: objects left one level above an existing deeper directory are invisible ('content not found') and a re-store duplicates them one level down, so today a mid-split crash, an rsync of a flat store into a split one, or 1.0.18 on Linux writing an uppercase-segment object loose in c4/ (portability) all hide objects. The invariant makes all three valid states, makes split an optimization, and removes two concepts (Folder as a separate store type = depth 0; split as a required writer behavior).

reader_rules: Lookup (deepest-first): dir = <store>; for k in 0..44: if a directory dir/lower(id[2k:2k+2]) exists, descend and continue; else stop. Then stat <dir>/<ID>; on a miss climb to each ancestor directory on the path and stat <ancestor>/<ID>, down to <store>/<ID>. First regular file found is the object. Never stat case variants of directory names on the fast path.
Has, Open, ContentPath and Remove all use the same lookup. Remove deletes the object at EVERY level where it exists (duplicates are legal, so a single delete is not a removal).

Walk enumerates every ID-named regular file at every depth, ignores names that do not parse as a 90-character C4 ID (journal, log.c4m, .ingest.*, .DS_Store, directories not 2 lowercase chars), and reports each ID once (dedupe by ID; content is identical by construction).

Legacy tolerance, time-boxed: readers in the 1.x line keep the 1.0.18 fold fallback (try ASCII case variants of each 2-character segment) ONLY after the any-depth lookup misses, so that un-normalized Mac (c4/4E/) and Linux exact-case (c4/4E/ beside c4/4e/) stores stay readable on case-sensitive volumes. On case-insensitive volumes the lowercase lookup already hits a 4E/ directory, so the fallback costs nothing there. It is retired in the first minor release after `c4 store normalize` has shipped and the 1.0.x line is unsupported; it is never consulted on a hit.

Never tolerated by the shared reader: the c4ts layout (c4/<88 characters without the c4 prefix>) and the c4d layout (<root>/<id[3:5]>/<ID>). Those stores are migrated by rename (below), not read in place.

Non-ID names in the store root are reserved for the implementation (journal, log.c4m, .ingest.*, any dotfile) and are ignored by Walk, never moved by split, and never returned by lookup. Readers must not assume the root holds only IDs and directories.
A reader may never infer or detect filesystem case sensitivity (ext4 casefold, ZFS mixed, NTFS per-directory make detection unsound); the lowercase rule is applied on every filesystem regardless.
writer_rules: Put: stream to a temp file in the store root named .ingest.<random> (dot-prefixed, shorter than 90 chars so the temp path is never the longest path), computing the ID while writing. Then under the store lock: run the reader lookup; if the object exists at ANY level, delete the temp file and return (no duplicate). Otherwise rename the temp file to <deepest existing directory on the lowercased prefix path>/<ID>. Put never creates a directory.

Two writers racing on the same ID: both rename to the same final path; rename is atomic and the bytes are identical, so either order is correct and neither may report an error on EEXIST-style outcomes. Two writers racing on the same shard directory on a case-insensitive volume: both use the identical lowercase name, so mkdir returns 'exists' to the loser, which must be treated as success (never as a conflict, never retried with another spelling). No writer ever creates a directory whose name is not exactly 2 lowercase ASCII base58 characters, so a both-case pair (4e/ and 4E/) can never be created by a conforming writer on any filesystem.

Split (optional optimization, default on in Go with threshold 4,096 ID-named files per directory): when the writer's own Put pushes directory D past the threshold, for each ID-named regular file f in D whose next segment s = lower(f[2k:2k+2]) (k = depth of D): mkdir D/s if absent (exists is success), then rename D/f to D/s/f. A failed rename leaves f in D, where it is still valid. Split moves ONLY names that parse as C4 IDs (fixes the master bug that moved journal to jo/journal), never touches dotfiles or other names, never recurses, and never deletes. Split may be interrupted at any point and the store remains valid.

Split in a store at depth 0 (flat root): the root splits into c4/ only; the next split of c4/ produces the id[2:4] level. This is the existing behavior and is kept (it is just the rule applied twice).

Writers that never split (imgbin, c4ts, c4d, any Swift or C implementation, a shell script using mkdir and mv) are fully conforming: they write to the deepest existing directory and read any depth. On FAT32 a non-splitting writer stops at 8,191 objects per directory; that is the filesystem's limit, not the format's.

Object-store writers (S3Store in c4 and c4d): key = <configured prefix><exact-case ID>, flat. No lowercased key levels; if a bucket must mirror a filesystem store file-for-file, mirror the filesystem layout verbatim (lowercase dirs, exact-case files) and the any-depth reader reads it.

Writers never write into, rename, or delete anything in the store root that is not an ID-named file or a 2-character lowercase directory, except their own temp files and the implementation's reserved files (journal, log.c4m).
migration: General: one new verb `c4 store normalize [--apply]` (dry-run by default, prints every rename; no interactive prompt; stderr narration, stdout data). It performs ONLY same-filesystem renames of directories and object files; it never copies bytes, never re-hashes (optional `--verify` re-hashes before pruning a duplicate), never deletes an object unless `--prune-duplicates` is given long-form, and can be interrupted at any point leaving a valid store because every intermediate state is valid under the any-depth rule.

Mac mixed-case trie (~/.c4/store, the Ash mirror: c4/4E/<ID>, 120 of 182 names non-lowercase): rename each non-lowercase directory to its lowercase spelling (case-only rename works in place on APFS; measured 120 renames in 0.05 s, 300/300 objects readable afterward with 1.0.18 and master). Zero object moves. The store is readable by 1.0.18, master, c4py and imgbin before, during and after. Never required: moving objects, touching log.c4m or .ingest.* leftovers.

Linux exact-case trie (a Mac store copied verbatim, or a Linux-native store that already has 4e/ beside 4E/): for each non-lowercase directory X in a parent P: mkdir P/lower(X) if absent; rename each ID-named file P/X/f to P/lower(X)/f, skipping f if the destination already exists (leave both; the lowercase one is canonical, the other is pruned only with --prune-duplicates after a size or hash check); rmdir P/X only when empty. Same filesystem, no bytes copied, interruptible. Do NOT normalize a Linux store that 1.0.18 (or master/c4py/imgbin) will still write to until a release with the new writer is installed there: 1.0.18 on Linux writes new uppercase-segment objects loose in c4/ (valid under any-depth, readable), but master/c4py/imgbin cannot see lowercase-dir objects on a case-sensitive volume (compat: ~41% invisible, and they duplicate).

master (unreleased v1.1) stores: same trie, plus two things. (1) If <store>/jo/journal exists (the split-moved journal), normalize concatenates jo/journal followed by the root journal (older entries first) into a new root journal written to a temp file and renamed into place, then removes jo/journal and jo/ if empty. (2) Forward-port the 1.0.18 fold fallback as the legacy reader. Fix split to move only ID-named files before shipping, or the bug recurs after normalization.

c4ts (<store>/c4/<88 chars>): normalize renames each file c4/<88> to c4/c4<88> in place (c4/ is on every ID's prefix path, so the result is valid at depth 1 immediately; no split needed). Rename only. c4ts code is rewritten to the rule (it is wrong today and reads nothing else).

c4d (<root>/<id[3:5]>/<ID>, exact case, .c4d-tmp-* temp files): the directories (e.g. EU/) are not on any prefix path. Normalize renames each object <root>/XY/<ID> to <root>/<ID> (flat, depth 0; valid immediately) and rmdir XY when empty; a later optional split deepens it. Rename only. c4d adopts the shared Go store package when revived; its own FileStore is deleted (one implementation per idea).

Mixed-depth stores from rsync merges or interrupted splits (objects at <store>/<ID> while c4/ exists, or c4/<ID> while c4/4e exists): no migration required at all; they are valid. `normalize` may optionally push objects to the deepest existing directory as a tidy step. Run tonight: 1.0.18 cannot see these objects and re-store duplicates them, so this case is a correctness fix delivered by the reader change alone.

Mirroring between machines: normalize on each machine with c4, never rely on rsync to fix names; rsync --delete-after/--delete-delay between stores whose shard names differ only in case wipes the shard (portability, exit 0). After both sides are lowercase every rsync/cp/tar/zip mode is an exact union.

Never required, for any layout: re-hashing content, copying object bytes, creating a store-format marker or version file, splitting, changing S3 keys, or taking the store offline (every intermediate state is readable by the new reader and, on Macs, by every old one).
conformance_vectors: Notation: vector = ID; store state; expected path (relative to store root). 'exists' lists the directories present. rejected_alternatives.alternative: Fixed one-level prefix toLower(id[0:4]) (182 dirs), toLower(id[0:5]) (6,370) or toLower(id[0:6]) (222,950), or two fixed 2-char levels
rejected_alternatives.why_rejected: Not readable by any existing tool (run: every `c4 cat` fails and every existing writer forks the store by writing a second copy at the root); migration moves all 194,127 objects. Each is unruly at one end: id[0:4] tops out ~10^7 (ext4 htree) and 1.5M on FAT32; id[0:5] puts a 1,000-object store in 914 directories; id[0:6] puts 10,000 objects in 9,721 directories and exceeds FAT32's 65,536-entry cap in one parent. Occupancy math shows no fixed width stays in the 100-50,000 band across 10^3-10^15.

rejected_alternatives.alternative: 1-character levels (35-way fan-out) to fix the split shape
rejected_alternatives.why_rejected: Fixes the 4,096/1,225 mismatch (117 objects per child after a split) but is a new format every existing store and reader must be migrated to (object moves, not renames), deeper paths (double the levels), and it was not measured. The shape problem costs enumeration time and directory count, never lookup time or correctness; it does not justify a clean break. Can be revisited as a writer-side choice if a future rule allows 1-char names, which the current rule does not.

rejected_alternatives.alternative: Raise the default threshold to 65,536 in the format
rejected_alternatives.why_rejected: Occupancy is better from 10^6 up (448-6,900 mean) but it exceeds FAT32's 8,191 objects per directory and exFAT's linear-scan comfort zone, and freezing any number in the format is unnecessary: under any-depth the threshold is writer-local, so a large-volume deployment can use 65,536 today via SetSplitThreshold with zero compatibility cost.

rejected_alternatives.alternative: Keep exact-case directory names and rely on the 1.0.18 tolerant lookup forever
rejected_alternatives.why_rejected: Leaves the 40% Linux defect in every non-Go reader, costs 11-13 stats per fold hit/miss (vs 4-6), and keeps the both-case pair (4e/ beside 4E/) possible, which is exactly what makes rsync --delete-after wipe a shard with exit 0 and breaks Dropbox, OneDrive, iCloud, Syncthing and rclone (portability).
Not locale-proof: 'i' uppercases to dotted İ under Turkish/Azeri locales. Lowercasing is safe because base58 has no 'I'.

rejected_alternatives.alternative: Detect filesystem case sensitivity and choose a spelling per volume
rejected_alternatives.why_rejected: Unsound: ext4 casefold is per directory, ZFS is per dataset, NTFS per directory (WSL), NFS inherits the server; a store moves between volumes by copy. One canonical spelling needs no detection.

rejected_alternatives.alternative: Top-down any-depth reader (stat root first, then descend)
rejected_alternatives.why_rejected: Measured: +2 stats on every hit at depth 2 (5 vs 3 at depth 1... 7 vs 5 at depth 3) with the same miss cost as deepest-first. Deepest-first is free on hits.

rejected_alternatives.alternative: A store-format marker or version file in the root
rejected_alternatives.why_rejected: A new concept that every implementation must write and check; it cannot be trusted anyway (verification over assertion: the reader can tell the layout from the directory names). The rule is self-describing: 2 lowercase chars per level, ID file at any depth.

rejected_alternatives.alternative: Drop the 'c4' level (shard directly by id[2:4] at the root)
rejected_alternatives.why_rejected: Forces moving every object in every existing store for a saving of 3 path characters, and mixes ID-named content with reserved root files (journal, log.c4m) in the sharded root.

rejected_alternatives.alternative: Keep c4ts's name-without-prefix files or c4d's id[3:5] directories as tolerated legacy layouts
rejected_alternatives.why_rejected: Each tolerated layout multiplies reader code across five languages; both migrate by pure rename to a valid any-depth state (c4/<ID> and <root>/<ID> respectively) in one pass, so tolerance buys nothing.

rejected_alternatives.alternative: Prefix routing across volumes/buckets inside the layout rule now
rejected_alternatives.why_rejected: Out of the format's scope: the lowercased prefix path is already a pure function of the ID, so a level-1 (182) or level-2 (222,950) routing table in MultiStore is the same rule one level up and can be added later as new code with no change to on-disk layout.

open_for_joshua: Adopt the rule as written: lowercased adaptive 2-character trie with any-depth validity (deepest-first reader) and the split threshold demoted from format to writer parameter. Everything else here follows from that one decision.

Which release carries it: v1.1 only, or also a 1.0.19 whose writer lowercases and whose reader honors any-depth, so that Linux stores can be normalized while 1.0.x tools still write to them (today 1.0.18 on Linux writes uppercase-segment objects loose in c4/; master, c4py and imgbin cannot read a lowercased Linux store at all).

Whether normalizing an existing store is an explicit `c4 store normalize --apply` (my recommendation: dry-run default, rename-only, no deletes without --prune-duplicates) or happens automatically on first write by a new tool. Automatic is tempting for Mac stores (120 renames, 0.05 s) but on a Linux store it may run while an old writer is still active.

Whether FAT32/exFAT remain targets. If not, the Go default threshold could be raised (65,536 gives a far better shape above 10^6) with no format consequence; if yes, 4,096 stays. Either way the number is not in the rule.

Whether the ugly middle band (10^6-10^7 objects: 141k-223k directories averaging 7-45, enumeration ~25x slower, lookups unchanged) is acceptable with the 4,096 default, or whether a 1-character-level variant should be studied as a future writer option (it would require widening the directory-name grammar and was not measured).

c4d: adopt the shared Go store package when revived (delete its FileStore), or delete c4d's store entirely. ShardedFolder (store/sharded.go) and the separate flat Folder type: delete both (Folder is depth 0 of the one rule).
Walk semantics for duplicates: silently report each ID once (proposed) versus exposing duplicates for a tidy verb. Affects c4sh's walkTreeStore and the gc paths.

Observed, out of scope: each `c4 id -s` call in 1.0.18 stores a second object besides the content (four extra IDs landed in c4/ during the run). If that is the per-call record c4m, confirm it is intended to live in the content store at all.

attacks.lens: Portability and transport: take the lowercased adaptive 2-char trie with any-depth validity across case-insensitive/case-sensitive volumes, tar/cp/ditto/rsync round trips, cloud sync, Windows names and path limits, FAT/exFAT; run on this Mac (APFS, c4 1.0.18) under /tmp/store-layout/attack-portability/.

breaks.scenario: The rule's Walk ('ignores ... directories not 2 lowercase chars') is applied to an existing un-normalized store, on this Mac, with no Linux involved. readdir returns the on-disk spelling (4E) even on case-insensitive APFS, so a grammar-filtered Walk skips every legacy directory. gc, verify, store-to-store copy and any 'report each ID once' consumer silently lose most of the store until normalize has run. 1.0.18's Walk (filepath.WalkDir, parse the file name, no directory filter) does not have this defect, so the rule as written is a regression.
breaks.evidence: Read-only count on the real store ~/.c4/store/c4 (182 dirs, 120 non-lowercase): `LC_ALL=C find ... -type f -name 'c4*' | grep -cE '/c4/[1-9a-z]{2}/c4'` = 40,755 of 194,139 objects (21%) are under a directory that matches ^[1-9a-z]{2}$; the other 153,384 (79%) would be invisible to the rule's Walk. (Also 75,067 = 38.7% sit in a dir whose spelling differs from their exact-case id[2:4], matching the ground's 39.8%.) 1.0.18 Walk source: release-1.0.x/store/treestore.go lines 328-345, no directory-name check.

breaks.scenario: Legacy uppercase shard directories silently absorb new writes forever on case-insensitive volumes, because the writer rule says 'mkdir returns exists ... must be treated as success'. Nothing in the rule ever renames the directory, and no transport fixes the destination spelling. The claim 'a both-case pair (4e/ and 4E/) can never be created by a conforming writer on any filesystem' is false across replicas: Mac replica keeps c4/4E/ under the new writer; copy it to Linux (verbatim, as every tool does); a conforming Linux writer mkdirs c4/4e/ beside it; the pair now exists, which is exactly the state that makes rsync --delete-after wipe a shard and that Dropbox/OneDrive/iCloud/Syncthing/rclone refuse (portability ground).
breaks.evidence: /tmp/store-layout/attack-portability/e1: `mkdir -p store/c4/4E; mkdir -p store/c4/4e` -> exit 0, `ls store/c4` -> 4E. `C4_STORE=.../e1/store c4 id -s in/v2.txt` (ID c44eNX6P..., exact-case segment '4e') landed at store/c4/4E/c44eNX6P... (find -type f). `tar -cf e1.tar -C store .` lists ./c4/4E/c44eNX6P... so Linux receives it under 4E. e12: `cp -R src/c4/ dst/c4/` and `ditto src dst` where src has c4/4e/ (normalized) and dst has c4/4E/ -> dst still spelled 4E afterwards, objects merged into it. Normalization never propagates by transport.

breaks.scenario: Mirroring between a normalized replica and a not-yet-normalized replica with rsync --delete-after (the migration section says 'normalize on each machine', which necessarily creates this mixed state for a while, and only warns about stores 'whose shard names differ only in case' without forbidding delete-after between replicas during rollout). The whole shard is deleted on the destination, including the object the source just sent, exit 0.
breaks.evidence: /tmp/store-layout/attack-portability/e2: src/c4/4e/c44eAAAA (normalized), dst/c4/4E/{c44EBBBB,c44eAAAA} (legacy Mac spelling). `rsync -a --delete-after src/ dst/` (rsync 3.5.0) -> exit=0, `ls -R dst` shows dst/c4 empty. Same command with plain `--delete` (e2b) produced the correct dst/c4/4e/c44eAAAA. Reproduces the ground's 1j/1J finding in the exact state the migration plan creates.

weaknesses: Archive spelling depends on how the path was typed, not on disk: `tar -cf e1b.tar -C store c4/4e` on the 4E directory wrote members as c4/4e/... while `tar -cf -C store .` wrote ./c4/4E/.... Transport can normalize or un-normalize a replica by accident; the rule should say the only truth is readdir spelling (os.ReadDir), and `c4 store normalize` must detect spelling via ReadDir, never via Stat/MkdirAll (which succeed on any case variant).

The legacy fold fallback as specified ('try ASCII case variants of each 2-character segment ONLY after the any-depth lookup misses') must run the full deepest-first any-depth lookup inside each variant subtree; 1.0.18's foldSearch (treestore.go 389-410) returns false at any interior node ('objects live in the leaves'), so forward-porting it verbatim would miss an object left one level above a legacy 4E/ subtree on a case-sensitive volume.

Windows writer race: os.Rename of the temp file onto an existing object can fail with a sharing violation (reader has it open), which is not an EEXIST-style outcome; the writer rule should say any rename failure is followed by a re-run of the lookup, and exists-at-any-level is success.

FAT32 stores a 2-char lowercase name as an 8.3 entry with the NT lowercase case bit; drivers or tools that ignore the bit (Linux vfat shortname=win95, old readers) report 4E. Not testable here (no disk images). Harmless on the FAT volume itself (case-insensitive) but a copy made through such a driver re-creates uppercase names on ext4.

A transport that folds FILE names (Samba 'preserve case = no' / 'default case = lower', DOS-era tools) silently changes the ID that Walk reports, since a lowercased 90-char name still parses as a C4 ID. Walk trusts names; the rule should note that only --verify (re-hash) is authoritative, per verification-over-assertion.

Finder drag of a store onto another store offers Replace (deletes destination contents) rather than Merge; lowercase names make this more likely to look like the same folder, not less. Already in the portability ground; the rule's mirroring text should mention it beside rsync.
survives: Exactly-2-character directory names at every level: no 2-character name can be a Windows reserved device name; 'c4' as the literal first level is safe; nothing to change.
ASCII lowercase folding of directory names only, exact-case 90-char file names: locale-proof (no 'I' in base58), NFC/NFD identity, ID recoverable from the file name, S3 keys unchanged. Do not touch.

Any-depth validity with deepest-first reading: every merge produced by cp -R, ditto, tar extraction and rsync -a (without delete-after) of a flat or shallower store into a split one is a valid state under the rule; this is the correct fix for the states 1.0.18 cannot see (confirmed in the draft run). Keep.
No marker/version file; split threshold outside the format; non-splitting writers conforming. Keep.
rsync --delete, --delete-before and --delete-during are correct even across case spellings (e2b: dst ended as c4/4e/c44eAAAA); only --delete-after/--delete-delay are destructive.
Path length: root + 3 per level + 1 + 90; at depth 4 (10^12-10^15 objects) root may be about 153 characters under Win32 MAX_PATH 260; not binding.
Flat S3 keys <prefix><exact-case ID>: correct, no directories, no case issue.
required_changes: Walk must enumerate every directory regardless of spelling (as 1.0.18 does), or at minimum every directory whose name case-folds to 2 base58 characters; the 'ignores directories not 2 lowercase chars' clause must go. Measured: it would hide 153,384 of 194,139 objects (79%) in the real store on this Mac today.

Writer rule for mkdir-exists: after MkdirAll/EEXIST the writer must confirm the on-disk spelling with one ReadDir of the parent (cached per directory) and, if the existing entry is a case variant, rename it to lowercase in place (case-only rename on the same volume; on a case-sensitive volume the variant is a different directory, so write into the lowercase one and leave the variant for normalize). Equivalently: a new writer normalizes every directory it touches. Without this, Mac replicas keep 4E/ indefinitely and the 'no both-case pair' guarantee fails the moment they are copied to Linux.

Migration/mirroring section: state that normalization never propagates by cp, ditto, tar or rsync (measured), so `c4 store normalize` must be run on every replica; forbid rsync --delete-after/--delete-delay between replicas until both are normalized (measured wipe, exit 0, in the rollout state the plan itself creates); recommend --delete (during) if deletion is needed; normalize must detect spelling via ReadDir, never Stat.

Legacy fallback spec: for each case-variant directory found at a level, run the full deepest-first any-depth lookup in that subtree (do not forward-port 1.0.18 foldSearch's interior-node early return).
Writer rule on Windows: any failure of the final rename re-runs the lookup; object present at any level = success (sharing violations are not EEXIST).
Note in the rule that Walk trusts names and only --verify re-hashing is authoritative, so name-folding transports (Samba preserve case = no) are detectable rather than silent.

attacks.lens: Compatibility and mixed versions: stores shared by c4 1.0.18, master, c4git/c4sh (older pins), c4py, imgbin, c4ts, and rsync/cp between a Mac and Linux. Everything below was run on this Mac (APFS, case-insensitive) with c4 1.0.18 (/opt/homebrew/bin/c4) and a master build (/tmp/store-layout/attack-compat/c4-master); script and full output: /tmp/store-layout/attack-compat/run.sh and results.txt; IDs from gen/ids.py (verified: attack-0 -> c423cnQf... matches `c4 -x`). Case-sensitive filesystems were not available (no disk images), so Linux claims are reasoned from code, not run. DISCLOSURE: one command in this run (`c4 store` typed in the release-1.0.x worktree, intended as a help probe) was interpreted by 1.0.18 as `c4 id -s store/` and wrote that directory's snapshot into the DEFAULT store ~/.c4/store (about 12 small source files plus a record). Nothing was deleted or modified there, but the read-only rule on ~/.c4 was broken by that one call; nothing was done to undo it.

breaks.scenario: The drafted Linux normalize procedure (mkdir P/lower(X); move files, skip if destination exists; --prune-duplicates after a size or hash check) run on a case-insensitive or casefolded volume deletes the only copy of every object in every non-lowercase shard.
breaks.evidence: Experiment B3: c4/4E/<LO> created; `mkdir -p c4/4e` succeeds (same directory); `[ -e c4/4e/<LO> ]` is true so the file is 'skipped, leave both'; `cmp c4/4E/<LO> c4/4e/<LO>` reports identical (the hash check passes); os.path.samefile reports True; after the prune step `rm c4/4E/<LO>` the directory c4/4e holds 0 files. The draft forbids filesystem case detection, so the normalizer cannot know which procedure it is on; it must treat 'destination exists' as a candidate duplicate only when os.SameFile is false. Note that ext4 casefold is per directory and NFS from a Mac is case-insensitive, so 'I am on Linux' is not a safe proxy either.

breaks.scenario: A root split by 1.0.18 OR master moves the reserved root files: log.c4m -> lo/log.c4m and journal -> jo/journal. The draft attributes this only to master's journal and the migration text only repairs jo/journal.
breaks.evidence: Experiment C: a root with 4,096 ID-named files plus `journal` and `log.c4m`, then one `c4 -s` (1.0.18) -> root entries `c4 jo lo`, files at ./jo/journal and ./lo/log.c4m. Same with master, which then starts a fresh root `journal` (root: `c4 jo journal lo`). The real ~/.c4/store has log.c4m at the root with no lo/ directory only because it was written after that store split. Consequence for mixed versions: as long as any 1.0.18/master/c4py writer can trigger a root split in a shared store, the reserved files move, and `normalize` must also fold lo/log.c4m back (and ignore/remove lo/, jo/). The rule's statement 'the only directories that may exist are those on some ID's prefix path' is violated by every shipped writer at the first root split.

breaks.scenario: Any old writer (1.0.18, master, c4py, imgbin never splits so exempt) that triggers a split in a lowercased store re-creates exact-case directory names one level down, so the invariant 'no both-case pair can exist' is only true if NO pre-rule writer ever splits the store again. On Linux this produces c4/4e/HN beside a new-writer c4/4e/hn, which is exactly the rsync --delete-after shard-wipe case the rule claims to have removed.
breaks.evidence: Experiment D: lowercased leaf c4/4e with 4,096 ID-named files, one `c4 -s` by 1.0.18 -> split created 1,131 level-3 directories, 932 of them non-lowercase (sample: 11 14 16 17 18 ... HN); the stored object landed at c4/4e/HN/<ID>. Readable on the Mac by both binaries (c4/4e/hn resolves to HN), but the store is no longer normalized the moment an old writer splits. The 'time-boxed' retirement of the fold fallback has no observable precondition because the rule (correctly) rejects a marker file; the only safe retirement condition is one `c4 store normalize` can verify at run time.

breaks.scenario: Mixed-depth merges (rsync -a or cp -R of a shallower store into a deeper one) hide objects from EVERY shipped reader and every re-store duplicates them one level deeper. The rule fixes this for new readers only; until old readers are gone, a new writer that follows 'write to the deepest existing directory' and leaves a shallower copy in place (e.g. after an interrupted split or a Remove that deleted only the deep copy) produces states old tools call 'content not found'.
breaks.evidence: Experiment A: flat store (2 objects) rsynced into a store with c4/4e, c4/2t, c4/23 -> `c4 cat` with 1.0.18 and master: 'content not found' for both root objects; deep object fine. Re-store with 1.0.18 wrote a second copy at c4/2t/<ID>; re-store with master wrote c4/<ID> (c4/4a absent); the root copies remain. Experiment F (cp -R, reverse order): object at c4/<ID> while c4/23 exists -> not found by both. This confirms the draft's own run; it is listed as a break because the rule's reader_rules say the state is 'valid' without saying it is INVISIBLE to c4git (pins v1.0.16), c4sh, c4py and imgbin, which will keep duplicating it.

breaks.scenario: Cross-process races produce the mixed-depth state today and the rule's writer text says 'under the store lock' as if that lock were cross-process. It is not: TreeStore uses an in-process sync.Mutex only, and no flock/LockFileEx exists in either store package.
breaks.evidence: grep for flock|Flock|LockFileEx over release-1.0.x/store and master store: no matches; treestore.go line 29 `mu sync.Mutex`. Two processes (c4 + c4git, or two c4 invocations) can interleave: process 1 computes path c4/<ID> (c4/4e absent), process 2's Put pushes c4/ past 4,096 and creates c4/4e moving the listed files, process 1 renames its temp file to c4/<ID> afterwards -> shallower object, invisible to old readers. Not reproduced tonight (timing), but it follows from the code; the any-depth rule is what makes it benign for new readers, and the rule should say so instead of implying a lock prevents it.

weaknesses: Duplicates at two depths with DIFFERENT bytes (a corrupt or truncated deeper copy beside a good shallower one): both 1.0.18 and master read the deepest copy and fail verification ('stored content ... ' / 'object failed verification'), never trying the good copy. Experiment E. The draft's 'content is identical by construction' is an assumption; the deepest-first reader should fall through to the next level on a verification failure, or `c4 cat` should (partial knowledge is valid; a good copy exists).

1.0.18 Walk is filepath.WalkDir over the whole tree: it reports IDs at every depth including ones Open/ContentPath cannot find, and reports a duplicated ID twice. Any gc built on old Walk + old Remove will try to remove an 'invisible' object and get ENOENT (Remove = os.Remove(path) then foldFind, which skips a level whenever a variant directory exists there). Under the rule old Remove also deletes only the deepest copy, so a shallower copy survives and the object 'reappears' to new readers after an old-tool gc.
The level-3 split shape is real, not just a model: one 1.0.18 split of a 4,097-object leaf produced 1,131 directories (3.6 objects each) on this Mac (Experiment D).

c4git pins c4 v1.0.16 (compat result; no fold fallback) and c4sh a pre-1.0.18 pseudo-version: on a case-sensitive volume they cannot read a normalized store at all (about 40% invisible) and duplicate on write. The draft lists this under open_for_joshua; it is a prerequisite, not an option: no Linux normalize until every Go consumer is on a reader that honors lowercase + any-depth.

The migration text for the Linux exact-case trie handles files in P/X only; a depth-3 Linux store (c4/4E/EA/<ID> beside c4/4e/ea/<ID>) needs the merge applied recursively, and rmdir P/X 'only when empty' will never be empty while subdirectories remain.
c4ts normalize (c4/<88> -> c4/c4<88>) is a pure rename as claimed, but any c4ts process still running reads nothing afterwards; the rewrite must ship first or in the same step.
survives: Case-only directory rename on APFS works in place with both `mv` and Go/Python os.rename (Experiment B: 4E -> 4e, one call, no copy); the Mac normalize path (120 renames, zero object moves) is sound and should not be changed.

Lowercased directory names are read and written correctly by both 1.0.18 and master on the Mac with no fallback (Experiments A/D/F: uppercase-segment IDs under lowercase dirs returned the right bytes); the lowercase-only grammar for 2-character names needs no tolerance code on case-insensitive volumes.

Deepest-first any-depth lookup is the right reader: in every mixed-depth state produced tonight (root-beside-c4/, c4/-beside-c4/xx, interrupted-split equivalents) the object is at a shallower level on its own prefix path, exactly what the invariant makes valid, and it also makes the cross-process split/Put race harmless for new readers.
Verification at read time caught the corrupt duplicate in Experiment E with both binaries; keep 'verification over assertion' as the backstop for any duplicate semantics.
Keeping the c4/ level, the exact-case object file name, flat S3 keys, and rejecting a marker file all held up: nothing tonight needed a marker, and every migration remained rename-only.

Split demoted to a writer-local optimization with a non-frozen threshold: nothing in the mixed-version runs depended on the threshold value, and a store at any threshold was readable by both binaries.
required_changes: normalize: treat 'destination already exists' as a duplicate candidate ONLY when os.SameFile(src, dst) is false; if SameFile, skip the file and the prune step entirely (the directory is the same inode). Never delete under --prune-duplicates without that check; add this as a conformance vector (V14: Linux-merge procedure on a case-insensitive volume loses nothing).

normalize: repair BOTH moved reserved files from any shipped writer's root split: lo/log.c4m -> log.c4m and jo/journal (+ root journal concatenation) -> journal; then remove lo/ and jo/ if empty. Reader rule: 2-character lowercase directories at the ROOT other than c4/ are never on a prefix path and are ignored. Writer rule: say explicitly that 1.0.18 and master (today's code) move every non-dot root file on split, so the reserved-files guarantee holds only for writers built on the new split.

Replace 'time-boxed' retirement of the fold fallback with a verifiable condition: the fallback is retired only when `c4 store normalize` (dry-run) reports zero non-lowercase directories, or simply keep it permanently (it is consulted only on a miss; the measured cost on hits is zero). State plainly that any pre-rule writer that splits re-creates exact-case names (932 of 1,131 in one split tonight), so a shared store is normalized only until the last old writer is retired.

Sequence the rollout as a requirement, not an open question: (1) ship a 1.0.19 whose writer lowercases and whose reader is deepest-first any-depth; (2) bump c4git, c4sh, c4-mcp, c4snap pins and port c4py/imgbin; (3) only then permit `normalize --apply` on case-sensitive volumes. Until (2), say in the rule that a normalized Linux store is unreadable (about 40%) by c4git v1.0.16, c4sh, c4py and imgbin.

Writer rule wording: replace 'under the store lock' with 'under the process-local lock; there is no cross-process lock, and the any-depth invariant is what makes concurrent split/Put interleavings valid'. Add a conformance vector for the race outcome (object one level above a directory created concurrently).

Reader rule: on a verification failure at the deepest copy, continue climbing and return the first copy that verifies (duplicates are legal, so bytes are NOT identical by construction); `c4 cat` and ContentPath follow the same order. Walk dedupes by ID but should expose the duplicate count to a tidy verb.

Migration text for case-sensitive stores must be recursive (merge P/X/* into P/lower(X)/* at every depth before rmdir), and must state that Remove by old tools deletes only the deepest copy, so `normalize --prune-duplicates` is the only way to retire shallow copies left by old gc.

attacks.lens: Simplicity, scale and cost (guardian of elegance; implementer of five ports)

breaks.scenario: The 'c4/' level is a wasted level that double-moves every object at the first split. Measured with the 1.0.18 store package (SetSplitThreshold 4096, /tmp/store-layout/attack-simplicity/harness, store s1): after 4,096 Puts the root split moved all objects into c4/ (files by depth {1:4097}); the very next Put split c4/ into 182 leaves (depth {1:1, 2:4097}, mean 22.4, max 39). Two consecutive Puts performed 8,192 renames; every store crossing 4,096 jumps from 1 directory to 185. The draft keeps the level for compatibility (correct) but the rule as written obliges a conforming splitter to pass through the useless depth-1 state.
breaks.evidence: ./harness/harness /tmp/store-layout/attack-simplicity/s1 4200 4096 -> 'after 4096 puts: dirs=3 ... files by depth: map[1:4097]'; 'after 4097 puts: dirs=185 nonempty=183 mean=22.4'. Fix is free under any-depth: a writer splitting a flat root may create c4/xx directly (objects at c4/xx are valid; no reader change).

breaks.scenario: Non-ID root files are moved by 1.0.18's split too, not only master's: with a 'journal' and 'log.c4m' in the root at threshold 8, 1.0.18 produced jo/journal and lo/log.c4m (dotfiles like .DS_Store were skipped because isTemp() is name[0]=='.'). It also counts them toward the threshold (root split fired at 4,096 objects + 1 journal). The draft's migration step for jo/journal is scoped to master and omits log.c4m.
breaks.evidence: store s2: 'journal at: /tmp/store-layout/attack-simplicity/s2/jo/journal', find -> s2/lo/log.c4m; release-1.0.x/store/treestore.go split(): skips only e.IsDir() || isTemp(name). ~/.c4/store has log.c4m at root and no lo/ (read-only ls), so the real store escaped only because log.c4m was written after the root had already split.

breaks.scenario: 'Threshold is writer-local, so FAT32 and a tidy shape are both available' is not true under a 2-character step. Recomputed: lowercased fan-out 1,225 (35x35, bin weights 1/2/4 of 3,364, 4.0x spread), level-1 182 bins; mean occupancy right after a deep split = threshold/1,225: 3.3 at 4,096, 53 at 65,536, 6.7 at the FAT32 maximum 8,191. A leaf of >=100 after a split needs threshold 122,500; >=1,000 needs 1.2M. So no FAT32-safe writer can ever have a tidy store above ~600k objects; the choice is FAT32 xor shape, and demoting the number to a writer parameter does not dissolve that. The draft should say so rather than present SetSplitThreshold as the escape.
breaks.evidence: python recompute (this run): '2-char folded bins 1225 ratio 4.0', 'thr 4096 ... after deeper split mean 3.34', 'thr 65536 ... 53.5', 'FAT32 cap allows threshold <=8191, which gives 6.69 per leaf'. Matches the scale result's 141k dirs averaging 7 at 10^6.

weaknesses: The path is NOT a pure function of the ID; the 45-element candidate set is. The draft is honest about this, but the reader rules then quietly add three derived concepts that a deepest-only rule would not need: Walk must dedupe by ID, Remove must delete at every level, Put must probe every level before writing. These are the real price of any-depth and should be listed as such in the rule, in one place, so each port implements the same three.

The 1.0.18 fold fallback is a tolerance list inside the reader. As drafted it is ambiguous whether it is part of the shared reader (which c4py, imgbin, c4ts, Swift and C would then have to carry: foldSearch + sameAsAny + foldVariants, ~50 lines each) or Go-only. master does not even have it today, so v1.1 would add it in order to retire it. Lowercase + any-depth already makes a Mac store readable everywhere; the fallback buys only 'read an un-normalized Mac copy on Linux before running normalize'.

Over-specification: 'deepest-first fixed as the reference' and 'readers never stat case variants on the fast path' are implementation guidance, not format. The format is two sentences (lowercase 2-char levels; object valid at any level of its prefix path). Keeping the two separated keeps the five-port conformance surface to the vectors V1-V13.

Small-store tidiness is only true below 4,096: at 4,097 objects the store is 185 directories averaging 22 (measured), and that is the tidiest the trie ever gets again (every deeper split lands at 3.3/dir). The draft's '1,000-object store has zero directories' is true but is the wrong number to quote.

Concurrent split vs an out-of-process reader produces a transient false miss under both 1.0.18 and the drafted deepest-first reader (file renamed out of D after the reader stated D/s/f and before it climbs to D/f). The in-process mutex does not cover a CLI + c4d pair. Not new, but any-depth does not fix it either; the rule should not claim 'split may be interrupted at any point' without 'by the writer'.

Grammar nit: the draft's V11 regex ^[1-9a-z]{2}$ is right (base58 has uppercase L, so 'l' appears after lowercasing) but the reasoning should be stated; a port author who knows base58 lacks lowercase l will exclude it.

normalize grows three flags (--apply, --verify, --prune-duplicates). --verify and --prune-duplicates are a second verb's worth of surface for a case (true duplicates at two levels) that only the mid-split-crash path can create; consider shipping normalize rename-only and leaving pruning to gc.
survives: Lowercased 2-character adaptive trie with the c4/ level kept: migrates by rename, every existing reader reads it, 2-char names dodge Windows reserved names; recomputed occupancy agrees with the scale result on every figure (182 / 6,370 / 222,950 bins, P(id[2]='6') = 2.3%, 4.0x deep-bin spread).

Any-depth validity: it turns the mid-split state, rsync merges and loose uppercase objects into valid states and removes Folder and mandatory split as concepts; the cost is the three derived rules above, not a format concept.
Threshold out of the format and no marker file: correct and should not be revisited.
ASCII lowercase only (no uppercase fold, no case-sensitivity detection) and exact-case object file names.
Rejection of fixed-prefix and 1-character layouts: the numbers hold; the 1-char option is the only thing that would fix the shape and it is a clean break.
required_changes: State the rule as two format sentences (lowercase 2-char prefix levels; object valid at any level of its own prefix path) and move deepest-first ordering, fast-path rules and the threshold into a separate 'reference writer/reader' section.
List the three derived obligations of any-depth explicitly as the conformance cost: Put probes all levels before writing, Walk reports each ID once, Remove deletes at every level.
Make the fold fallback Go-1.0.x-only and not part of the shared reader; v1.1 ships `c4 store normalize` and no fallback (master has none to retire). If kept, say which ports carry it.
Writer rule for splitting a flat root: create c4/xx directly rather than passing through c4/ (allowed by any-depth; zero compat; removes the measured 8,192-rename double move and the dirs=3 state).

Replace the 'use SetSplitThreshold 65,536 on APFS/XFS/ZFS' escape with the plain statement: under a 2-char step no FAT32-safe threshold yields more than 6.7 objects per leaf after a deep split; FAT32 support and tidy occupancy above ~600k objects are mutually exclusive, and the default 4,096 chooses FAT32.

Migration: note that 1.0.18 (not only master) moves any non-dot root file on a root split (jo/journal, lo/log.c4m) and counts it toward the threshold; normalize should restore any non-ID file found at <store>/xx/<name> to the root, not just jo/journal.
Qualify 'split may be interrupted at any point' as a single-writer guarantee; the cross-process reader race is unchanged by the rule.
